newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Stocks fall leaves gold, commodities cold.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Stocks fall leaves gold, commodities cold.

text.p: Dark clouds over Wall Street failed to send investors running for shelter in the gold market, where prices were just modestly firmer on Monday.
The weakness in equities also appeared to have had scant impact on other commodity markets.
Investors, rattled by gold's decline to 12-year lows this year, have shunned the former "safe haven" despite a 250-point plunge on the U.S. stock market last Friday.
"They are very wary of gold. It's been a dreadful investment," said analyst Ted Arnold of Merrill Lynch.
"If they are worried about the stock market falling and want a safe haven, they'll go in to cash for a time and then maybe bonds, but it's not going be gold."
Even worse for gold bugs, underhedged producers are increasingly worried about locking in profits and have taken to selling into any small rally.
Gold was fixed in London at $326.05 an ounce on Monday morning, compared to $324.65 on Friday afternoon - dead in the centre of a recent $320-$330 price range.
"A lot of currencies are no longer backed by gold," said a senior commodities dealer. "Gold is becoming more of a normal physical commodity."

Wall Street's drop did prompt some investment funds to buy back some of their "short" positions in the gold market, resulting in the mild rise. But heavy producer selling countered any upside potential.
Ongoing concerns about possible U.S. interest rate rises in future and the prospect of central banks selling some more of their gold reserves have further dampened enthusiasm for gold.
"If we do get a rate rise you'll see gold down on producer selling rather than see it climb on the back of a stock exchange fall," one dealer said.
In other commodities, base metals were down sharply last Friday and on Monday. But several traders said equities markets were not the main spark for the losses seen in the industrial metals.
Copper for three month delivery on the London Metal Exchange (LME) sank to six-month lows on Friday and extended the downtrend on Monday.
Copper was last at $2,158 per tonne on Monday morning, down $55 from Friday's close, bringing the two-day loss to $100, or about 4.5 percent.
"It didn't really have much to do with the shares," one trader said on Monday.
"Only if there's a general economic downtrend, if major economies really went into recession, would base metals prices be hit," he added.
Copper had been looking vulnerable in recent weeks as supplies became more available. LME stocks have more than doubled this year to 260,875 tonnes, with the bulk of the rise seen in July.
On Monday, aluminium and zinc got caught up in copper's slipstream, also seeing losses.
The soft commodities were seasonally quiet.

Coffee and cocoa failed to show much immediate reaction to Wall Street although sugar was sharply higher after a strong rally in New York on Friday. But traders attributed to the move to chart-based fund buying rather than a direct link to the stock market.
